title: India's Biggest Trade Deal Ever Takes Effect in 16 Days. Here's What Changes for the Diaspora.
excerpt: The India-UK Free Trade Agreement launches July 15 with steep tariff cuts, extended pension portability for professionals, and a steel dispute that almost sank it.
body:
India's most comprehensive trade agreement ever is about to become real. On July 15, the India-UK Free Trade Agreement will enter into force — just twelve months after it was signed, making it the fastest implementation of any trade deal Britain has ever completed.

Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal, speaking at UK-India Week 2026 in London last Friday, put it plainly: "Every trading relationship and every partnership stands on its own legs. The UK Free Trade Agreement is going to be the most comprehensive agreement that India has entered into so far, and it will come into force in July."

## What the Deal Actually Does

The numbers are substantial. The UK government estimates the FTA will boost bilateral trade by £25.5 billion annually in the long run and add £4.8 billion to UK GDP. Bilateral trade between the two countries has already grown from roughly £17 billion when UK-India Week launched a decade ago to nearly £48 billion today.

The tariff cuts are where it gets specific. Whisky tariffs — long a sticking point — will drop from 150% to 40%. Automotive tariffs fall from 100% to 10% under a quota system. Cosmetics tariffs of up to 22% will be eliminated, either immediately or over ten years.

On the other side, the UK will cut tariffs on Indian goods including clothing, footwear, and some food products, potentially lowering costs for British consumers and importers.

## Why the Diaspora Should Pay Attention

The deal includes a provision that directly affects professionals moving between the two countries. Under the new UK-India Double Contributions Convention Agreement — entering force alongside the FTA — British and Indian professionals working in each other's countries can continue building entitlement to their home country's pension for up to 60 months, extended from 36 months, without double-paying social security contributions.

This matters for the estimated 1.6 million people of Indian origin in the UK and the thousands of professionals who shuttle between London and Mumbai, Bengaluru, and Delhi for work. The provision covers highly skilled professionals on pre-existing visa routes, mirroring arrangements the UK already has with Japan, Korea, and Canada.

For NRIs in the UK and those considering a move, the practical upshot is simpler: work in one country, keep building your pension in the other, for longer.

## The Steel Hurdle That Almost Derailed It

Getting here was not straightforward. The deal hit a significant snag earlier this year when Britain unveiled stricter steel import safeguards, set to take effect from July 1. India's trade secretary Rajesh Agrawal called the steel measures a "sticking point" that was not factored into the original negotiations.

The curbs threatened to dilute market access benefits that Indian steelmakers expected from the FTA's tariff reductions. For weeks, implementation looked like it might slip to autumn.

But both sides pushed through. UK Trade Secretary Peter Kyle described the effort as working "at breakneck speed," while Goyal characterised the discussions as productive. The steel issue was ultimately handled separately from the FTA implementation, clearing the path for the July 15 launch.

## A Bigger Picture

The timing is noteworthy. India is simultaneously negotiating a separate trade deal with the United States — one that Goyal says is "very close" — while also managing a recently signed EU trade pact expected to take effect early next year. The UK deal arriving first gives British exporters what the UK government calls "an immediate competitive advantage" over other markets, since India has never implemented an FTA of this scale before.

For India, it is a test of whether the country can execute complex trade agreements at speed, a capability that will matter as it pursues deeper integration with multiple Western economies simultaneously.

UK-India Week 2026 closed with a message that both governments clearly want to land: the FTA is not an endpoint, but a platform. Whether that platform delivers depends on what businesses on both sides actually do with it starting July 15.

*Sources: UK Government (gov.uk), Reuters, India Global Forum / PR Newswire*
